articles.title: Dream Big, Build India - Brighter Kashmir
articles.summary: Dream Big, Build India  Brighter Kashmir
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call to India’s youth to dream big, think differently and live without fear for a Viksit Bharat by 2047 is more than a motivational message.
It is a reminder that the country’s future will be shaped by the aspirations, skills, courage and determination of its young generation.
India stands at a defining moment.
With a large youth population, expanding digital infrastructure and growing opportunities in science, technology, entrepreneurship and innovation, the country possesses enormous potential to emerge as a global leader.
But demographic strength alone cannot guarantee national progress.
Young people must be equipped with quality education, employable skills, equal opportunities and the freedom to question, create and innovate.
The vision of a developed India must extend beyond economic growth and impressive infrastructure.
It should mean dignified employment, accessible healthcare, quality education, social justice, clean surroundings and equal opportunities for every citizen.
Development becomes meaningful only when its benefits reach villages, small towns, disadvantaged communities and families struggling to secure a better future.
The Prime Minister’s emphasis on thinking differently is particularly relevant in an era when artificial intelligence, automation and technological disruption are transforming economies.
India cannot depend solely on traditional employment models.
It must encourage entrepreneurship, research, vocational education and practical learning.
Schools and universities should nurture problem-solvers rather than merely produce degree-holders.
However, asking young people to dream big must go hand in hand with addressing their concerns.
Unemployment, examination pressures, recruitment delays, inadequate career guidance and the widening gap between academic qualifications and market requirements continue to frustrate many aspiring Indians.
Their ambitions need institutional support, transparent recruitment systems, affordable education and a business environment that rewards innovation.
Young people also need the courage to challenge social prejudices, reject communal hatred, protect the environment and uphold constitutional values.
A developed nation cannot be built through economic indicators alone; it requires responsible citizens, strong institutions and a culture of tolerance and accountability.
The responsibility, therefore, is shared.
The government must create opportunities, educational institutions must prepare students for the future, industries must invest in skills and innovation, and families must encourage independent thinking.
Young Indians, in turn, must embrace discipline, hard work and social responsibility.
The journey towards 2047 will not be completed through slogans or declarations.
It will demand sustained reforms, measurable outcomes and collective commitment.
India’s youth must dare to dream, but the nation must give those dreams the means to become reality.
That is the true foundation of a Viksit Bharat.

articles.title: 'Army is the rule, army is the law': India tears into Pakistan at UN over minority rights - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'Army is the rule, army is the law': India tears into Pakistan at UN over minority rights  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: India on Sunday accused Pakistan of using allegations about the treatment of religious minorities in India to divert attention from its own record on minority rights, judicial independence and press freedom.
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly's Sixth Committee during discussions on the rule of law at national and international levels, Mythili R, a counsellor at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, accused Islamabad of preaching legal accountability abroad while undermining it at home.
She described Pakistan as a country where "the army is the rule and the law", alleging that judicial independence had been weakened, civilians were being tried in military courts and political opposition was being suppressed.
"At the UN, Pakistan lectures others on the rule of law. Yet at home, the Army is the rule, and the Army is the law. Judicial independence undermined, civilians tried in military courts, political opposition suppressed," she said, according to a statement shared by India's Permanent Mission to the UN on X.
India slams Pakistan's record on minorities 
Mythili also challenged Pakistan's claims on minority rights, pointing to what she described as a steady decline in the proportion of minorities in the country's population since its creation.
She questioned press freedom in Pakistan, referring to the Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines issued by its Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Under the guidelines, foreign media outlets must obtain a "No-Objection Certificate" to report freely outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi.
The Indian diplomat accused Pakistan of repeatedly failing to uphold the rule of law and said its focus on India was misplaced.
"The rule of law bestows an obligation upon those in positions of power to do good for those they govern. However, in the case of Pakistan, unfortunately, this promise is broken again and again. It is not India that has an obsession with Pakistan but the other way round," she said.
India defends Operation Sindoor
The exchange also brought the two countries' sharply contrasting positions on cross-border terrorism into focus. Mythili defended India's response to the Pakistan-backed terror attack in Pahalgam last year, which killed 26 people, describing Operation Sindoor as measured and proportionate.
She urged Pakistan to stop repeating what she called baseless allegations against India, arguing that doing so would not shield its representatives from accountability for promises made to their own people.
"Reading and re-reading the same laundry list of false allegations against my country will not absolve Pakistani representatives of the promises that they have made to their people and which they have no intention to keep," she said.
Taking a swipe at Pakistan's claims about the outcome of the military confrontation, she added, "As far as the result of the same is concerned, if bombed airfields and destroyed hangars are victory, they are welcome to enjoy it," she said.
India warns against nuclear blackmail
The latest exchange followed India's response on Saturday to Pakistan's remarks at the UN General Assembly's First Committee, where discussions included disarmament and international security.
First Secretary Anmol Sher Singh Bedi said India's military posture was defensive and guided by its own security requirements, rather than directed against any particular country. He defended India's response to the Pahalgam attack as "measured, targeted, and non-escalatory" and an exercise of its right to self-defence.
Bedi laid out India's position on terrorism and the risk of nuclear escalation, stating, "First: Any terrorist attack against India will receive a fitting response; Second: India will not bow to nuclear blackmail; Third: India will make no distinction between those who sponsor terrorism and those who mastermind it."
He argued that states could not escape responsibility for supporting militant groups by acting through non-state actors, adding that such actions did not diminish India's right to defend itself.
"Escalation concerns are best judged by conduct, over rhetoric. Nuclear weapons must not be a routine instrument of statecraft. Relying on a nuclear overhang to limit the consequences of sub-conventional activity raises escalation risk, not restraint," he said.
Bedi also criticised what he described as a recurring pattern in regional crises, involving provocation, denial of responsibility and calls for restraint after retaliation.
He said, "where those in power are neither elected by nor accountable to the people, crisis becomes an instrument of power and instability becomes useful."
Reaffirming India's stated commitment to peace, Bedi said the country did not seek conflict but would respond to threats. He concluded, "without accountability for reckless actions, peace merely becomes a pause between crises."

articles.title: China, EU reach deal to curb surge in Chinese hybrid car exports - India's News.Net
articles.summary: China, EU reach deal to curb surge in Chinese hybrid car exports  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
BEIJING, China: China and the European Union have reached an agreement that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars to the bloc by more than half, marking a significant step in efforts to address the EU's widening trade deficit with Beijing.
The "shared understanding" would "moderate" China's exports of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU and cut imports by several million cars over four years, European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said on October 9, without detailing how the agreement would be implemented.
The understanding followed two days of discussions between Sefcovic and Chinese officials, including Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, after years of disputes over China's growing goods shipments, particularly cars.
"I came here with one clear purpose: to start rebalancing the EU-China trade relationship and to make sure this first phase of negotiations under the trade and investment consultations delivers its first tangible outcomes," Sefcovic told a press briefing.
The EU's trade deficit with China cost the bloc more than one billion euros (US$1.12 billion) a day last year, according to EU data.
Wang told Sefcovic that China was not the root cause of the EU's problems but a partner in solving them, according to China's commerce ministry.
The two sides also reached understandings to improve EU products' access to Chinese markets and facilitate China's export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, Sefcovic said.
EU officials have been concerned by a sharp rise in Chinese car imports. Plug-in hybrid imports into the EU rose 86 percent in the year to September, while prices fell 20 percent. More than half of these vehicles now come from China, compared with China's 30 percent share of plug-in hybrid electric vehicle imports by value in 2025.
China and the EU also agreed to continue discussions on price undertakings and review procedures related to the EU's anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese electric vehicles.
Their dispute over cheap Chinese EV exports dates back to 2024 and has since expanded to brandy, pork and dairy as well as rare earths and critical minerals.
As part of the consensus, China's commerce ministry said it would continue facilitating export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets through a "green channel" mechanism.
Chinese shipments to the EU totaled $560 billion last year, up from $517 billion in 2024, according to UN Comtrade data. China imported $268.3 billion of European goods, down from $269.4 billion a year earlier.
The two sides will continue exploring possible tariff reductions on certain goods within WTO rules and discussions on market access for medical devices. Their next regular consultation meeting is scheduled for March 2027.

articles.title: Su-57 Still Under Review, IAF Boss Says. Can India & Russia Replicate BrahMos Success Story with Felons? - EurAsian Times
articles.summary: Su-57 Still Under Review, IAF Boss Says. Can India & Russia Replicate BrahMos Success Story with Felons?  EurAsian TimesRussia offers India 140 Su-57E stealth fighters amid Rafale deal  prameyanews.comRussia is ready to give India the source code for the Su-57E radar  Первый техническийSu-57: Can Russia's 5th-gen fighter plug India's fighter jet gap?  Moneycontrol.com
articles.full_text:
Unlike the F-35, India has received a formal offer from Russia for the Sukhoi Su-57 fifth-generation fighter but has not yet decided whether to evaluate it, the head of the Indian Air Force said.
Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh told reporters on the sidelines of the Exercise Tarang Shakti in Jodhpur that the Indian Air Force was aware of Moscow’s proposal.
“As far as the Su-57 is concerned, we have received information that an offer has been made, but no decision has been taken on whether to evaluate it,” he said.
“Once a decision is made, we will assess how well it meets our requirements.”
Russia has repeatedly pitched the Su-57 to India.
Earlier, as EurAsian Times reported, Russian President Vladimir Putin personally renewed the Su-57 offer to India.
Speaking on the sidelines of the St. Petersburg Economic Forum, Putin reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to cooperate with India on the Su-57 the aircraft.
“It’s fifth-generation technology — I think it’s the best in the world as of now,” the Russian President said at the forum.
President Putin recalled Indo-Russian 5th-gen aircraft collaboration and said: “As far as the Su-57 goes, at one point we proposed to our Indian friends to work together on this technology. “But back then, our Indian friends said: ‘Go ahead on your own, and then we will see – maybe we’ll join’…The aircraft could have been our joint project. We built it independently, but we are ready to work with India in this field – to supply this aircraft and to keep developing it,” the Russian President told the reporters. “We don’t have any issues with it or any limitations. The same goes for air defense systems,” he added.
The Su-57 is a supersonic, twin-engine fifth-generation aircraft designed to destroy air, ground, and naval targets. Developed to compete with the F-22 and F-35, the ‘Felon’ jet features enhanced stealth through composite materials and can cruise supersonically.
It is a multi-role fighter jet capable of air superiority missions, ground attacks, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare. Russia is integrating a range of lethal weapon systems on the Su-57 platform, including the long-range R-37M missile and hypersonic missiles, as reported by the EurAsian Times.
Additionally, the aircraft is being integrated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enhance threat detection, decision-making, and pilot support. However, these features have failed to attract buyers, especially India.
If India proceeds with the Su-57 deal and Moscow meets all Indian prerequisites, including technology transfer, it could inject billions into Russia’s sanctions-hit economy. India would also get an interim fifth-gen fighter till the indigenous AMCA arrives.
Russia’s defense exports have historically benefited through high-profile deals with India. An excellent example is the Su-30MKI, India’s customized variant of the Su-30.
India’s acquisition of the Su-30MKI in the early 2000s influenced other nations, such as Malaysia, which modeled its Su-30MKM on the Indian version. Its versatility—including thrust-vectoring engines, canards, and integrated avionics from multiple countries—made it a flagship for Russian technology.
Another bigger success story is the BrahMos supersonic missile.
India’s DRDO and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya launched the joint venture in 1998 to develop and produce the BrahMos, one of the world’s fastest supersonic cruise missiles.
The Philippines was the first customer of the BrahMos, signing a contract worth approximately $375 million with BrahMos Aerospace in January 2022 for three shore-based anti-ship missile batteries.
The package, intended for the Philippine Marine Corps, includes mobile launchers, missiles, operator and maintainer training, and integrated logistics support. Deliveries began in April 2024 with the first battery and continued through 2025 and into 2026, with the third and final battery nearing completion.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro has indicated interest in further adapting or expanding the capability to suit the country’s geography and operational needs.
The two countries also reached an agreement on air-to-air missile cooperation that “enhances technology collaboration and defense capabilities”, he said.
Indian PM Modi hailed the “growing trust” between Jakarta and New Delhi after meeting Prabowo, which he said underpinned cooperation in “defense, security and maritime affairs”.
“Today, we reached an agreement to enhance defense exchanges, disaster management, and industrial cooperation,” Modi told reporters.
Earlier, the BrahMos missile system from India.
The Indian Navy inducted its first BrahMos system in 2005 aboard INS Rajput. The Indian Army followed in 2007 with its own regiments, and the Air Force later introduced an air-launched version from the Su-30MKI in 2019.
The BrahMos missile saw combat use during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when Indian forces employed air-launched variants from the Su-30MKI. IAF reportedly fired 15-19 BrahMos missiles.
The Indo-Russian missile could have more export customers.
India sketched a list of “friendly nations” it deemed potential buyers, including the Philippines, Vietnam, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and South Africa. The list has since changed, with several countries dropping interest and others queuing up to assess the combat-tested missile system.
India reportedly started talks with Vietnam to sell off the supersonic cruise missile in 2023. An official with BrahMos Aerospace Ltd told the EurAsian Times at the time: “Vietnam had shown interest in the system. But the negotiations have just started.”
Further evidence of BrahMos’s widespread appeal in Southeast Asia is Malaysia’s interest in the missile system, particularly the air-launched variant, which could be integrated with the Royal Malaysian Air Force’s Su-30MKM fighter jets.
By 2025, Malaysia appeared in lists of countries “queuing up” or actively negotiating for BrahMos. In fact, in August that year, reports suggested Malaysia had begun preliminary negotiations with Russia and India for the missile, aiming to revolutionize its Indo-Pacific airpower projection.
Besides Southeast Asia, the Middle East could be a potential market for the BrahMos missile.
Alexander Maksichev, Co-Director of BrahMos Aerospace, explicitly emphasized the UAE as a potential customer. Additionally, India has repeatedly listed the UAE among “friendly nations” eligible for BrahMos exports.
Other countries that have reportedly shown interest in the missile include Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, and Egypt. BrahMos has also gained traction in South America, with countries such as Brazil, Chile, Argentina, and Venezuela showing interest.
The Indo-Russian BrahMos is a major export success, and Putin may want to replicate that success with the Su-57, using Russian tech and Indian co-production and marketing.
Whether India will bite the bullet remains to be seen.

articles.title: Audi India mulling local production of electric car, aims to double market share in 3-5 years - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Audi India mulling local production of electric car, aims to double market share in 3-5 years  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Audi India is considering local manufacturing of a battery electric vehicle, with a decision expected in the next few months. The luxury carmaker aims to double its market share from around 8% to 15-16% over the next three to five years through new product launches, customer-focused initiatives and dealership expansion, particularly in tier-II and tier-III cities.
Audi India is considering local manufacturing of a battery electric vehicle (BEV), with the luxury carmaker betting on a three-pillar strategy to double its market share in the segment over the next three to five years to 15-16 per cent, a top company executive said.
In an interview with PTI, Audi India Brand Director Balbir Singh Dhillon outlined its strategy for India, centred on three key areas: customer centricity, new product introductions, and network expansion, to double its market share in the luxury car segment from around 8 per cent.
The German automaker is also looking to leverage the proposed India-EU free trade agreement (FTA) to bring more models to India to test market demand, while expanding its dealership network, particularly in tier-II and tier-III cities.
Elaborating, he said, "So we intend to double our market share in the next three to five years. Customer centricity, new products, and network expansion-put together, we believe should give us doubling of our market share in the next three to five years."
The proposed India-EU FTA could enable Audi to introduce more models in India at more competitive import duties and test their sales potential before considering local manufacturing, Dhillon said.
"FTA will help us bring more models to India for testing the volumes," he said.
Dhillon said the company would continue to rely on local manufacturing for its core portfolio, while imports could help expand the range of vehicles available to Indian customers.
He also pointed to the potential for the proposed EU-India free trade agreement (FTA) to create export opportunities for the wider Indian automotive industry.
"We will also get an opportunity to export the car, not Audi per se, but the Indian automotive industry, and you know we are opening up 95 per cent of the markets on both sides..
Audi plans to focus most of its dealership network expansion on tier-II and tier-III cities going forward, including entering new towns and converting some existing facilities into new-car showrooms.
"So most of the development that we will do in the next year to increase our network will be in tier-two and tier-three cities. We will enter new towns...We will convert some of our facilities, which already are there, into new car showrooms," Dhillon said.

articles.title: What was the Chemistry Nobel Prize given for? | Explained - The Hindu
articles.summary: What was the Chemistry Nobel Prize given for? | Explained  The HinduWhy mirror-image molecules matter in chemistry and commerce  IndiatimesKagan and Soai Win Chemistry Nobel for Solving Life’s Molecular Mirror Mystery  Kashmir LifeThey made chemistry choose a mirror image  NobelPrize.orgHenri Kagan, Kenso Soai win 2026 Nobel for controlling chirality  NewsBytes
articles.full_text:
STORY SO FAR: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for showing that it is possible to amplify a molecule’s “handedness,” and direct it in a way that it can be used to produce pharmaceutical products of a very high purity. Their work also offers clues to explaining how life on earth could have evolved from simple molecules.
Your left and right hand have the same number of fingers with ring fingers and thumbs on both of the same length yet why is that you can’t wear the left hand’s glove on the right? The reason is ‘chirality,’ from the Greek kheir, hand. Many chemical molecules that make up substances, including the organic molecules that make up things like DNA, also possess this property of chirality. The mirror-images of a molecule, the left and right-glove so to say, are called ‘enantiomers.’ Paradoxically the organic molecules that make up living organisms are overwhelmingly either left-handed or right-handed and in nature do not present themselves in 50:50 proportions. This property, of ‘homochirality,’ is as if a fashion house decided to base its entire business on making only left-handed gloves and accessories customised to it. Or as we observe, most people are right-handed and urban fixtures like door-knobs, car wipers and a whole lot of implements seem actively biased against left-handed people.

articles.title: Nobel peace laureate calls US sanctions on International Criminal Court 'unacceptable' - Dawn
articles.summary: Nobel peace laureate calls US sanctions on International Criminal Court 'unacceptable'  DawnNobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'  BBCThe Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifies  The GuardianHow the ICC can be saved  Al JazeeraTrump misses out on Nobel Prize again and imposes new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. What does it mean?  Th...
articles.full_text:
Jurist and former UN rights chief Navi Pillay, the winner of this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, on Saturday called sanctions announced by the US on the International Criminal Court (ICC) “unheard of” and “unacceptable”.
“There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague,” Pillay said via video link from Nuremberg during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo, lamenting “there are hundreds of staff who feel they are under threat”.
“Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable,” the 85-year-old South African lawyer said.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee on Friday announced that Pillay, who once sat on the ICC, was this year’s recipient of the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize.
Both the United States, whose leader Donald Trump has long coveted the award for himself, and ally Israel condemned her being awarded the honour.
Hours after Pillay was named the laureate, the United States announced new sanctions against the ICC, provoking swift condemnation from member states and the United Nations.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he described as a “rogue court”, escalating a long-running campaign by Trump’s administration against the Hague-based tribunal.
‘History will judge’
The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that “history will judge this moment”.
In addition to serving on the ICC, Pillay was the UN human rights high commissioner from 2008 to 2014, and headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which found last year that genocide was occurring in Gaza. The body does not speak on behalf of the UN.
Israel has rejected the COI’s findings, calling them “distorted and false”.
Israel’s foreign ministry said the award legitimised “anti-Israel hatred”, adding that it thought that Nazi propagandist Joseph Goebbels must be “applauding from hell”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the awarding of the prize to Pillay showed the Nobel committee had “lost its moral compass” by honouring “a bigot”.
Trump, who last month called on ICC member states to quit the court, meanwhile labelled the committee’s choice as “a disgraceful and embarrassing decision”, telling a rally of his supporters in Syracuse, New York, he had “never heard of” Pillay.

articles.title: India-US Trade Deal: Changed Circumstances to Shape Final Pact, Says Piyush Goyal - Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.summary: India-US Trade Deal: Changed Circumstances to Shape Final Pact, Says Piyush Goyal  Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.full_text:
Sandeep Patel
Piyush Goyal says changing circumstances will shape the final India-US interim trade pact as India seeks lower tariffs for its goods in the American market.
Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said that changing circumstances will be taken into account while finalising the proposed interim trade agreement between India and the United States, signalling that negotiations will continue as both countries assess the evolving trade environment.
Speaking to members of the industry chamber PHDCCI on Saturday, October 10, Goyal said the framework for the agreement had been announced in February, but developments since then would influence the final outcome.
“The US trade pact was announced in February. Some circumstances have changed, and the final agreement will be concluded keeping those developments in mind,” Goyal said, according to Press Trust of India.
The minister did not specify which developments had prompted the reassessment. However, changes in the United States' tariff framework have affected negotiations on the first phase of the proposed bilateral trade agreement (BTA).
India Seeks Competitive Tariffs in the US Market
A key priority for India is to secure lower tariffs on its goods than those imposed on competing countries selling similar products in the American market.
Tariff levels influence the final price of imported goods and can affect exporters' competitiveness. More favourable tariff terms could help Indian businesses compete with suppliers from other countries, while higher duties could make their products more expensive for American buyers.
India's position reflects the importance of securing market access on terms that support exports and protect the interests of domestic industries.
The final arrangement will depend on the outcome of negotiations and the tariff conditions applicable when the agreement is concluded. Goyal did not provide a timeline for finalising the pact or disclose the specific tariff concessions being discussed.
February Framework and Ongoing Negotiations
India and the United States announced a framework for an interim trade agreement in February 2026. The two countries have been working towards a broader trade arrangement intended to improve market access and address trade-related concerns.
The latest comments indicate that the February framework will not necessarily determine every element of the final agreement. Instead, negotiators will take account of the circumstances that have changed since the initial announcement.
The discussions are significant for Indian exporters seeking more predictable access to the US market. The United States is an important destination for Indian goods, and tariff changes can influence trade flows across several sectors.
The eventual agreement will depend on the terms accepted by both governments, including the treatment of Indian exports and the broader balance of concessions.
India Pursuing Trade Agreements With Other Partners
Goyal also said India was negotiating trade agreements with several other countries and regional groupings. These include Israel, Chile, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).
The parallel negotiations form part of India's wider effort to expand trade opportunities, diversify export markets and strengthen commercial relationships with different regions.
An agreement with the GCC could be significant for Indian businesses seeking access to Gulf markets, while negotiations with Chile and Israel could create opportunities in other sectors. Discussions with the EAEU would involve a regional economic grouping led by Russia.
However, negotiations with each partner are at different stages, and the minister's remarks did not establish a common timetable for concluding these agreements.
Exporters Await Clarity on Final Terms
Goyal's comments leave the final shape and timing of the India-US interim trade agreement open as negotiations continue. For exporters, the central issue is whether the eventual terms will offer Indian products a competitive position in the American market.
Lower tariffs relative to competing countries could improve price competitiveness, but the practical benefits will depend on the products covered, the extent of tariff concessions and the conditions attached to the agreement.
The government has not announced the final terms or a confirmed signing date. Further clarity is expected only when both sides reach an agreement on the outstanding issues.

                India’s Infrastructure Transformation: From Connectivity to Capacity
                प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 19:12 PM
            
                
 Building the Foundation of Growth
India’s infrastructure landscape has undergone a major transformation over the past 12 years. From transport and logistics to housing and water, infrastructure development has moved towards integrated planning and large-scale expansion. This has strengthened connectivity, improved access to essential services and created the foundations for sustained economic growth. Public capital expenditure has risen from about ₹2 lakh crore in FY 2014–15 to ₹12.2 lakh crore in FY 2026–27, supporting this advancement.                                                                                                                                                    
 A New Era of Rail Mobility 
Indian Railways is moving towards faster, safer and more modern mobility. Electrification, advanced safety systems, high-speed rail and new-generation trains are reshaping the rail network.
	- Railway budget increased from ₹32,000 crore in 2014–15 to ₹2.78 lakh crore in FY2026–27. 
- Rail electrification increased from about 20% before 2014 to 99.6% by July 2026. 
- 162 Vande Bharat, 2 Vande Bharat Sleeper Services and 72 Amrit Bharat services have improved connectivity and travel experience. 
- The Kavach Version 4.0 has been commissioned on 2,633 route km as of July 2026.
- The Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail Corridor is being developed over a 508 km route with a design speed of 350 kmph.
- Of the 1,340 stations identified under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, redevelopment has been completed for 261 stations as on 18 July 2026.
- First indigenously developed Hydrogen Fuel Cell Trainset has been launched in July 2026. It is a 10-coach train with capacity for around 2,600 passengers, running on the Jind–Sonipat section. It generates its own electricity onboard with water vapour and heat as the only by-product.
 
 
 
 Roads and Highways Connecting India
A wider and more capable road network is bringing regions closer. The expansion of National Highways, rural roads and major corridors is enabling smoother movement of people and goods.
	- India has the world’s second-largest road network at 63.73 lakh km. 
- Length of national highways increased by about 61%, from 91,287 km in FY 14 to 1,46,572 km in March 2026. 
- The length of four-lane and above national highways increased from 18,371 km in 2014 to 45,516 km. 
- The length of roads increased from 3.86 lakh km during 2000–2014 to 4.11 lakh km during 2014–2026 under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana. Since September 2024, PMGSY-IV has been launched with an objective to provide connectivity to 25,000 unconnected habitations by the year 2029.
- Under Bharatmala, 22,590 km of roads have been completed till 31 March 2026.
 Bridges and Tunnels: Engineering New Frontiers
Engineering breakthroughs are overcoming some of India’s most demanding geographical challenges. These projects are opening new routes across difficult terrain.
	- Chenab Bridge (2025): World's highest railway arch bridge, standing 359 m above the Chenab River; 1,315 m steel structure strengthening Jammu–Srinagar connectivity. 
- Anji Khad Bridge (2025): India's first cable-stayed railway bridge, in Jammu & Kashmir. 
- Pamban Bridge (2025): India's first vertical-lift railway sea bridge, connecting Rameswaram to the mainland; 2.07 km with a 72.5 m vertical lift span. 
- Z-Morh/Sonamarg Tunnel (2025): 12 km tunnel providing all-weather access through avalanche-prone terrain in J&K, improving movement towards Ladakh. 
- Sudarshan Setu (2024): 2.32 km bridge connecting Okha with Beyt Dwarka, Gujarat. 
- Atal Tunnel (2020): 9.02 km — world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet, connecting Manali and Lahaul-Spiti.
- Dr. Syama Prasad Mukherjee Tunnel (2017): 9 km all-weather tunnel between Jammu and Srinagar, cutting travel time by ~2 hours. 
 Civil Aviation and Regional Air Access
Air connectivity is reaching more cities, towns and remote regions. The expansion of airports, UDAN routes and digital passenger services is making flying more accessible across the country.
	- UDAN connected 95 airports, heliports, and water aerodromes through 679 routes, benefiting over 1.68 crore passengers as on 15 July 2026. 
- Operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 165 in July 2026.
- 25 greenfield airports have been approved after 2014.  
- Digi Yatra is active at 38 airports. The app has enabled over 10 crore seamless journeys with over 2.4 crore downloads.  
- Modified UDAN has been approved in March 2026 for FY 2026–27 to FY 2035–36 with an outlay of ₹28,840 crore, envisioning 100 new airports and 200 modern helipads to strengthen last-mile regional air connectivity.
 Metro: The Rise of Mass Urban Transit
India’s urban mobility network is expanding in scale and scope. Metro connectivity now spans more cities, while innovative systems are opening new possibilities for urban transport.
	- Metro network expanded from 248 km in 2014 to over 1,155 km in 2026.  
- Cities with metro connectivity increased from 5 to 26, while daily ridership crossed 1.15 crore passengers. 
- Kolkata operationalised India’s first underwater metro tunnel in 2024. 
- Kochi operationalised India’s first Water Metro system with the first boat launched in December 2021.
 India’s Maritime Momentum
India is strengthening its maritime backbone to support a growing economy and expanding trade. Investments in ports, waterways and maritime infrastructure are creating a more capable and connected ecosystem.
	- Major ports’ cargo handling capacity nearly doubled from 873 MMTPA in 2014 to 1,728 MMTPA in 2026. 
- Vessel turnaround time improved from 94 hours to 48.8 hours in 2025-26. 
- Major ports collectively handled 915.17 MT of cargo during FY 2025-26, increasing from 581 MT in FY 2014-15.
- The Sagarmala Programme strengthened port-led development, coastal connectivity, and logistics integration.
- National waterways increased from 5 in 2014 to 111 in 2026, of which 32 are operational. 
- India became the world's No. 1 ship-recycling nation in 2025, with its global share rising from 30.1% (2024) to 35.4% (2025) — recycling 2.99 million gross tons (GT), up nearly 60% from 1.86 million GT in 2024.
- Jawaharlal Nehru Port ranked 22nd as per the Container Port Performance Index (CPPI) 2025, published by the World Bank.
-  Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool (BMIP) has been launched on 12 May 2026. It is a USD 1.5 billion domestic insurance pool with a sovereign guarantee of USD 1.4 billion (₹12,980 crore), covering Hull & Machinery, Cargo, Protection and Indemnity, and War risk for Indian-flagged/controlled vessels. As on 29th July 2026, a total of 1608 policies covering Cargo War risks and Hull War risks have been issued under the Pool.
 Strengthening Logistics and Industrial Capacity
Infrastructure is increasingly being planned as an interconnected network supporting industry and trade. From GatiShakti to industrial corridors, the focus is on improving coordination, efficiency and manufacturing capacity.
	- PM GatiShakti National Master Plan integrated infrastructure planning across 58 Ministries and Departments using over 3,291 data layers. 
- As on 11 August 2026, 396 infrastructure projects with a total estimated cost of about ₹18.66 Lakh Crore have been evaluated through the Network Planning Group mechanism. Out of these, 256 projects have been sanctioned and 198 projects are under implementation. 
- The National Logistics Policy has strengthened multimodal logistics efficiency and supply chain integration.
- PRAGATI reviewed 382 projects worth over ₹85 lakh crore and resolved 2,958 issues.
- Over 4,220 industrial parks are mapped on the India Industrial Land Bank (IILB).
	- 272 plug-and-play industrial parks are operational across the country.
- 20 industrial smart cities have been approved across 7 industrial corridors.
- The BHAVYA scheme has been approved in March 2026 to develop 100 new plug-and-play industrial parks. 
- BHAVYA Rasayan Scheme has been approved on 24 July 2026, with an outlay of ₹3,030 crore. The scheme will be implemented over five years, from FY2026–27 to FY2030–31. 
- 7 Pradhan Mantri MITRA Parks have been proposed to strengthen the manufacturing ecosystem.
 Water, Housing and Urban Development
The infrastructure push extends directly to people’s homes and everyday needs. From tap-water access and affordable housing to urban renewal, these efforts are shaping better living conditions across rural and urban India.
	- Under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), rural tap water coverage increased from 3.23 crore in 2019 to around 15.91 crore households as on 10th August 2026.
- JJM 2.0 has been approved in March 2026. The mission has been extended to December 2028, with an enhanced outlay of ₹8.69 lakh crore. 
	- Under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban (PMAY-U), 99.25 lakh houses have been completed as on 12 August 2026. Around 96% of houses under PMAY-U 2.0 are allotted to women.
- Under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Grameen (PMAY-G), out of the 3.91 crore houses sanctioned, 3.13 crore houses have been completed as on 12 August 2026.  Nearly 75% of the houses sanctioned under PMAY-G are either in the name of women or under joint ownership.
- The SWAMIH Fund launched in 2019 delivered over 63,000 homes, benefiting around 2.52 lakh people as of June 2026.
- Under AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0, projects worth about ₹2.79 lakh crore have been sanctioned since 2015. 
- Under Smart Cities Mission, a total of 7,790 projects worth ₹1,56,257 crore have been completed as of March 2026.

“The U.S. and India announced in February that they had reached a framework for an interim trade agreement, but circumstances have changed, and the pact will be finalised accordingly,” Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Saturday (October 10, 2026).
He also said trade pact negotiations are on with number of regions including Israel, Chile, GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) and Russia-led group Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).
"USA (trade pact) February me announce hua. Thodi paristhitiyan badli hain, usko abhi madde nazar rakhte hue final hoga. (It was announced in February. Some circumstances have changed; the final decision will be made keeping that in mind)," Mr. Goyal said in New Delhi while addressing members of industry chamber PHDCCI.
India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods than its competitors in the American markets. The Minister did not elaborate about those circumstances, but the changing tariff landscape in the U.S. has led to further negotiations about the first phase of bilateral trade agreement (BTA) between India and the U.S.
Mr. Goyal earlier this month met U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on the sidelines of G20 trade Ministers meeting in Milwaukee. Both discussed trade pact-related issues.
Further, the Minister said that negotiations for a trade pact with Canada are moving at a faster pace and talks for an agreement with South Africa-led SACU group will start soon.
Several countries are keen to negotiate trade agreements with India, he said adding talks with Mexico will be launched next week. Mr. Goyal informed that the trade Ministers of the U.K. and Canada will be visiting India next week. India and the U.K. implemented a trade agreement in July. The U.K. Minister will be here for the India-U.K. Joint Economic and Trade Committee (JETCO) meeting.
Piyush Goyal criticises Opposition
The Union Minister slams Congress leader Rahul Gandhi for his claims and statements after meeting President Droupadi Murmu.
"It was an objectionable behaviour ... He has insulted the President ... This is a sense of anarchy," Mr. Goyal said, adding that the Opposition leaders have misbehaved with security personnel.
A delegation of INDIA bloc leaders met President Murmu on Friday evening (October 9, 2026) and handed her a memorandum on the alleged "vote chori".

CHENNAI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday reaffirmed the union government’s commitment to Tamil Nadu’s development, assuring the state of continued support and cooperation to accelerate its growth.
“Viksit Tamil Nadu will lead to Viksit Bharat (Developed TN will lead to a developed India),” Modi said while addressing a gathering on the IIT Madras campus after inaugurating and launching development projects worth over Rs 13,000 crore across the state, including the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project built at a cost of around Rs 4,900 crore.
Sharing the stage with Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, Modi described the occasion as a historic day for Tamil Nadu and said the projects spanning metro rail, highways, railways, ports, petroleum and scientific research would improve connectivity, strengthen industries and create employment opportunities.
Emphasising cooperative federalism, the prime minister said the centre’s commitment to Tamil Nadu would remain unchanged despite changes in the political leadership. Recalling his association with former CMs J Jayalalithaa, M Karunanidhi, O Panneerselvam, Edappadi K Palaniswami and M K Stalin, Modi said, “Governments and political leaderships may change, but our commitment to the people of Tamil Nadu and the rapid development of this great state remains unshakeable. Today, we take this journey forward together with Chief Minister Joseph Vijay ji.”
‘Indian talent giving solutions to global health challenges’
Stressing that national progress depended on the development of individual states, Modi highlighted India’s expanding metro network, which has grown from around 250 km in 2014 to over 1,100 km across 25 cities.
“These projects are not merely slabs of concrete and steel,” he said, adding that they would ensure faster commutes, smoother trade logistics, better industrial connectivity and employment opportunities for TN’s youth.
Earlier, he visited Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras and interacted with the researchers. He lauded the institution’s groundbreaking launch of high-resolution 3D cellular mapping of more than 100 human brains across different lifespan stages, along with the release of the “C-STROKE” digital atlas for stroke research.
Such breakthroughs, he said, prove that Indian talent is no longer merely adapting foreign innovations, but pioneering solutions to global healthcare challenges. The PM also launched highway projects worth around Rs 3,700 crore and railway infrastructure projects exceeding Rs 750 crore.
Port-related projects at Chennai, Kamarajar and V O Chidambaranar ports are expected to strengthen cargo handling and logistics. Modi also laid foundation stone for the Lube Oil Base Stocks project at Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited’s Manali refinery. He also offered prayers at a Shiva temple on IIT campus.

articles.title: India’s Techade drive: Five key moves in chips, electronics, AI and global competition - Newswav
articles.summary: India’s Techade drive: Five key moves in chips, electronics, AI and global competition  Newswav
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI, Oct 12 — India has committed billions of dollars in semiconductors, electronics manufacturing and artificial intelligence in a bid to become a global technology powerhouse.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi said at a groundbreaking ceremony for a chip assembly and testing facility that “this decade is India’s ‘Techade’”.
But it faces a long road to match the output of rivals like the United States, China and South Korea.
Here are five key things to know about India’s technology push:
Chips: ‘national priority’
From 2017-2025, India imported about US$150 billion worth of microchips — components that power everything from smartphones to weaponry.
New Delhi has pledged more than US$20 billion in government support to reduce that dependence.
Five assembly, testing and packaging plants are now in commercial production, involving US industry titan Micron, Indian firms Kaynes, CDIL and Suchi Semicon, and CG Semi, an Indian, Japanese and Thai joint venture.
But such facilities do not require the same expertise as core manufacturing and research.
Another seven projects have been approved, including from Tata Electronics, which is building a chip factory in Gujarat in partnership with Taiwan’s PSMC.
India’s semiconductor market, estimated at about US$50 billion in 2026, is projected to reach US$110 billion by 2030, and more than US$200 billion by 2035, according to government figures.
New Delhi calls building up semiconductor production “an urgent national priority”.
Electronics
India’s electronics production rose from about US$31 billion in 2014-15 to US$133 billion in 2024-25, according to the government, which wants the country to become a tech manufacturing hub.
Global manufacturers including Apple and Samsung have expanded production in India, as companies seek to diversify supply chains beyond China.
New Delhi is also trying to encourage local supply chains through incentives for component makers.
Data centres
India generates vast quantities of digital data but has only about three percent of global data-centre capacity, according to government figures.
India believes it can provide “an alternative” to existing options, said Arvind Gupta, head of the Digital India Foundation think tank.
The government says projects worth nearly US$70 billion are under construction, with a further US$90 billion announced.
Investors include Indian conglomerates Reliance and Adani, as well as US tech giants Amazon, Microsoft and Meta.
The southeastern port of Visakhapatnam is a key centre, where Google is building a US$15 billion AI hub.
Workforce strength
The world’s most populous nation says it has nearly 20 per cent of the global chip-design workforce.
Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw says about 70,000 design engineers have been trained in the past four years.
Authorities have expanded semiconductor-related courses and programmes across hundreds of engineering colleges.
Modi, speaking to global technology firms at a semiconductor conference in New Delhi in September, said that “such a huge talent pool is a goldmine”.
But Nomura, a Japanese investment bank, calls India “ground zero” for AI-driven job disruption in Asia, given its huge workforce and vast IT-services sector.
India’s AI push has fuelled job-loss concerns, but the government expects AI-linked jobs to nearly double to 1.25 million by 2027.
Uphill task
Experts question whether India can translate ambitious plans into a competitive technology ecosystem.
“India... has to navigate the complicated geopolitics of technology,” Gupta said, adding it faced three key challenges.
Those are “access to global capital”, as well as “attracting and retaining top global talent” and “sourcing the hardware resources that are the foundation to these technologies”. — AFP

CHENNAI : Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on Sunday inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for various development projects worth over ₹13,000 crore across Tamil Nadu. The initiatives included those in the road and rail transport and petroleum sectors.
The PM, along with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for the developments projects at an event held at the IIT Madras.
The projects include those in National Highways worth around ₹3,700 crore, initiatives in the Chennai Port, Kamarajar Port and V O Chidambaranar Port and Amrit railway stations. He also dedicated to the nation, the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre (SGBC) at IIT Madras.
Focusing on the strategic modernization of maritime logistics, the Prime Minister announced that the nation’s port infrastructure is being heavily bolstered to push the shipping sector to unprecedented heights, with Tamil Nadu playing a central role. He highlighted a recent landmark decision to invest approximately 17,000 crore rupees to transform Thoothukudi’s VOC Port into a World-Class Mega Container and Green Energy Hub, capable of accommodating ultra-large container vessels. “This will help Tamil Nadu become a global hub for industry and transport,” asserted Shri Modi.
Highlighting the operational successes of this maritime focus, the Prime Minister pointed out that both the speed and efficiency of Indian ports have drastically improved in recent years. He noted that significantly reducing ship turnaround times by half has allowed domestic products to reach global markets much faster than ever before. “Because of this, India’s products as well are able to reach global markets faster than before,” observed Shri Modi.
Earlier, PM Modi inaugurated the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project, built at a cost of around ₹4,900 crore.
PM Modi and CM Vijay together flagged off the new services and travelled on the Metro train. The new services are covered under Corridor four of Phase two of the Metro Rail project. In the newly inaugurated stretch, there are a total of 11 elevated Metro Stations covering approximately 15 km.
Turning to the blue economy, the Prime Minister underscored the vital role of fishermen in the nation’s Ocean Economy vision. He detailed that thousands of crores have been approved for Tamil Nadu through the PM Matsya Sampada Yojana and other schemes to upgrade fishing harbors, develop landing centers, and improve cold chain facilities. . “Help has also been provided to purchase transport vehicles to keep fish fresh,” noted Shri Modi.
Elaborating on the targeted support provided to coastal communities, the Prime Minister listed several key interventions, including the modernization of the Chennai Fishing Harbour and the development of a ‘Sea-weed Park’ in the state. “Through the Kisan Credit Card, working capital is now also easily available to fishermen,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Celebrating the tangible results of these targeted maritime policies, the Prime Minister proudly announced that national fish production has increased rapidly, driving seafood exports to their highest ever levels in terms of both quantity and value last year. “This is also improving the lives of our fishermen families and people in coastal communities,” asserted Shri Modi.
Concluding his address with a unified vision for the future, the Prime Minister pledged the absolute, unwavering commitment of the central government to assist Tamil Nadu in reaching continuous new heights of prosperity. He called for a collective effort to realize the grand vision of a developed nation by first ensuring a fully developed Tamil Nadu, offering his best wishes for the success of all the newly launched projects. “Together, we will realize the resolve of a Viksit Bharat through a Viksit Tamil Nadu,” affirmed Shri Modi.

articles.full_text:
Last Updated on October 11, 2026 9:21 pm by INDIAN AWAAZ
AMN / CHENNAI
Prime Minister Narendra Modi today inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for a series of development projects worth more than 13,000 crore rupees across Tamil Nadu at an event held at IIT-Madras.
The projects span road and rail transport, port infrastructure, petroleum and scientific research. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay was also present on the occasion. The projects include National Highway works worth around 3,700 crore rupees, initiatives at Chennai Port, Kamarajar Port and V. O. Chidambaranar Port, and the development of railway stations under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme.
Addressing the gathering, Prime Minister Modi described the inauguration of projects worth 13-thousand crore rupees in Tamil Nadu as a historic occasion, saying the initiatives will improve connectivity, strengthen industry and trade, and create employment opportunities for the state’s youth. Mr. Modi said the projects will make daily travel easier and support the state’s economic growth.
Recalling his interactions with former Tamil Nadu Chief Ministers M. Karunanidhi and J. Jayalalithaa, Mr. Modi said he had also worked with former Chief Ministers O. Panneerselvam, Edappadi K. Palaniswami and M. K. Stalin during his tenure as Prime Minister. He said that despite changes in governments, his commitment to the development of Tamil Nadu and the welfare of its people had remained unchanged. He added that he would continue this journey in cooperation with Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay.
Recalling his journey in public service, Mr. Modi said he had completed 25 years as head of government, having taken the oath as Gujarat Chief Minister in October 2001 before becoming Prime Minister. Mr. Modi said India’s progress draws strength from its rich cultural heritage, scientific achievements and modern infrastructure. He cited Tamil Nadu’s temples, scientific institutions and Metro rail network as examples of how tradition and modern development can go hand in hand. The Prime Minister also extended Navaratri greetings to the people of the state.
Mr. Modi also dedicated to the nation the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras. The centre is part of a pioneering scientific initiative to map more than 100 human brains and create three-dimensional atlases at cellular resolution. The research will cover the entire human lifespan, from the foetal stage to old age.
The Prime Minister also released C-STROKE, a unique atlas of the human brain affected by ischaemic stroke. Featuring more than 1,000 annotated microscopic sections, the atlas is expected to help researchers worldwide identify new targets for treatment.
Earlier in the day, Mr. Modi inaugurated the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase Two of the Chennai Metro Rail Project, built at a cost of around 4,900 crore rupees. The Prime Minister and Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay jointly flagged off the new Metro services and travelled on the train.
The newly inaugurated stretch is part of Corridor Four of Phase Two. It includes 11 elevated Metro stations spread across approximately 15 kilometres. The projects are aimed at strengthening transport connectivity, improving infrastructure and advancing scientific research in Tamil Nadu.

articles.full_text:
The malicious use of AI, particularly its potential role in developing bioweapons, has been identified alongside nuclear conflict as an existential threat
Nuclear conflict and the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI), including the development of bioweapons, are among the threats that could potentially lead to human extinction by 2100, according to a report called The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health, released by the general medical journal.
The study placed these dangers in the highest category of a pyramid ranking hundreds of potential threats to humanity, including diseases, injuries, socioeconomic drivers and other risks. The category comprises threats considered capable of causing human extinction by the end of the century.
Also Read | Should AI labs be treated like the owners of dangerous animals?
The malicious use of AI, particularly its potential role in developing bioweapons, has been identified alongside nuclear conflict as an existential threat. Nuclear conflict could have devastating consequences extending beyond immediate casualties, including the possibility of nuclear famine, while the misuse of AI could introduce new dangers through its application in the development of biological weapons, the study said.
The commission's framework categorises threats according to their potential scale of harm, placing human extinction risks at the top of the pyramid, followed by major catastrophic threats, major risks and causes, and the wider threat landscape.
“We divided hundreds of potential threats (diseases, injuries, socioeconomic drivers, and other threats) into a pyramid of threats with four categories: threats with the potential to lead to human extinction by 2100, major catastrophic threats, major risks and causes, and the wider threat landscape (figure 1). Threats with extinction potential, which represent the first category of the pyramid, include nuclear conflict with nuclear famine and the malicious use of AI, including bioweapons development,” the report read.
Also Read | Google researcher says AI may 'kill us all' in exit post: ‘We might be running out of time’
The study distinguished these existential threats from 15 major catastrophic threats that could cause extensive harm to human health and societies. These include air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, climate change, the collapse of development assistance for health, conventional conflict, high alcohol consumption, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics not enabled by AI, obesity, poor mental health, smoking and unhealthy ageing.

articles.title: Wisconsin couple rejects $131,000 offer for proposed data centre power line that threatens their trees, s - The Times of India
articles.summary: Wisconsin couple rejects $131,000 offer for proposed data centre power line that threatens their trees, s  The Times of IndiaMKE County: Board Approves New Transmission Line, Despite Data Center Fears  Urban MilwaukeeREAL ESTATE | Fredonia homeowner vows to fight ATC power line proposal  Washington County InsiderWisconsin homeowner vows to fight proposed data-center power line after utility offered $81,000 plus $50,000 to clear a 1,000-by-75-foot corridor and remove...
articles.full_text:
Wisconsin homeowner Jerry Zelenka has rejected a $131,000 offer from American Transmission Company (ATC). The money was offered for a proposed power line that would cross his property in Fredonia, Wisconsin, to supply electricity to a planned data centre in nearby Port Washington. Zelenka said the latest proposal calls for clearing mature trees, demolishing six buildings and placing a 130-foot transmission tower near his driveway.
The company has offered $81,000 in compensation for the property impacts, along with an additional $50,000 one-time payment if he signs an agreement now. The 75-year-old homeowner, who bought the land with his wife in 1990, said the proposed changes would leave their house standing while removing much of the property they have built and maintained over the years.
Proposed power line threatens trees and buildings
Zelenka said ATC's latest proposal follows an earlier application that, according to him, the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin deemed incomplete. The company has since submitted a new application with revised plans and routes.
Under the current proposal, Zelenka said, a stretch measuring about 1,000 feet long and 75 feet wide would be cleared of trees and vegetation. The affected trees include cedar, oak, ash, elm and black walnut. 
He also said the project would require removing a shed, chicken coop, hog barn, antique barn, garage, and machine shed.
“The point is that everything from that fence all the way to the road is clear-cut,” Zelenka said. “And after they clear-cut it, then they want to spray herbicide and just kill everything between my house and the highway.”
The proposed tower and high-voltage lines would also change the property's surroundings, potentially affecting its value.
“My house is right there. The only thing that’s left standing is the house,” he said.
Homeowner questions $131,000 compensation offer
Zelenka said the proposed compensation wouldn't cover the cost of replacing the buildings or adequately account for the impact on the property's value. He also objected to the additional payment being conditional on signing an agreement immediately.
“You know, the bribe in a sense is that if I were to sign up now, they’re offering $50,000 more,” Zelenka said.
The homeowner said relocating was not a realistic option for him and his 73-year-old wife, who has advanced Parkinson’s disease. The couple built their home after buying the land in the winter of 1990, spending nine months on the house while living in a shed.
Zelenka said he would not voluntarily accept the proposal and raised concerns that ATC could use eminent domain to acquire the property if they could not reach an agreement.
“If they decide they’re going to go this way, they can file for eminent domain, they’ll condemn the property, and there’s nothing I can do about it,” Zelenka said. “Then they’ll make an offer for whatever they feel is acceptable, and my only option at that point is I can fight them in court for a higher value, but I can’t stop the land seizure.”
Dispute over data centre power line continues
Zelenka questioned whether the proposed transmission line qualifies for eminent domain, arguing it would primarily serve a private data centre rather than the general public. He said two neighbouring property owners who are attorneys are challenging the issue in federal court. The legal outcome and the project's final route remain uncertain.
The homeowner also said changing proposals and compensation offers made ATC's plans hard to understand.
“The thing that’s really frustrating is trying to get the truth or accurate information,” he said. “First we get offers and then the offers are pulled and we think they’re routing another way… then, oop… now they’re sending new offers.”
Zelenka said he intends to continue opposing the proposed route rather than accept the compensation and fight it in court.

articles.title: Poland holds emergency security meeting over possible attack on PM Donald Tusk, defence minister - The Times of India
articles.summary: Poland holds emergency security meeting over possible attack on PM Donald Tusk, defence minister  The Times of IndiaPoland's police warn of a possible plot to attack Prime Minister Donald Tusk  The HinduPoland detains man suspected of planning assassination of PM Tusk  BBCPolish police detain man over threat to PM and defence minister  ReutersDonald Tusk says man accused of plotting to kill him detained  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Polish security services were due to hold an emergency meeting on Sunday after police received information about a possible attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, authorities said.
The exact nature and origin of the reported threat were not immediately clear. The meeting was ordered by interior minister Marcin Kierwiński and Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister-coordinator of special services, according to a statement posted on X by Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka.
“Following information received by the Polish Police regarding a possible attack ...interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, and the minister-coordinator of Special Services, Tomasz Siemoniak, have ordered action to be taken in this matter,” Galecka wrote.
She said a meeting would take place at 11 am local time at the Internal Security Agency’s Counter-Terrorism Centre.
Private broadcaster Radio Zet reported that police had received an email containing information about the threat.
As per news agency AP, police had received information about a possible attack, but authorities had not released further details.
Poland on alert after attacks at schools
The security alert comes as Polish authorities remain on high alert following a series of violent incidents at schools in the central Mazovian province over four days last week.
Three attacks left one person dead and several others injured, including children. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school wounded nine people, including fellow students, teachers and passersby, with a sharp object. He was arrested nearby.
The following day, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and wounded two other people in a knife attack at his former school. On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman wounded three people at a post-secondary school in Warsaw.
By Sunday morning, police had detained 117 people across Poland for carrying knives or other dangerous weapons, or for threatening attacks against schools or fellow students. Authorities had checked around 64,000 schools, according to AP.
Speaking at a crisis meeting with government and security officials on Sunday, Tusk said the school attacks were “spontaneous acts” driven by the online “glorification of violence”.
“We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale,” he said, adding that authorities had observed a rise in the fascination with violence both in Poland and globally.
Tusk said some of those detained were active in far-right circles. He also pointed to increased online searches for Nazi-related content and mass killers who had become idols on the internet.
Concerns over wider security threats
Poland has also raised concerns about security risks linked to its proximity to the war in Ukraine. In September, Tusk warned that Russia was likely to intensify hybrid attacks against Nato’s eastern flank.
In August, police detained a 23-year-old man accused of calling for the assassination of senior Polish politicians, Reuters reported.
Tusk had also said in 2024 that he received threats following the assassination attempt on Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico.
The latest security meeting comes amid concerns about possible copycat violence following the school attacks. Rumours of coordinated incidents and further attacks on what was described online as “bloody Friday” had circulated in parents’ online groups and mainstream media.
As a result, 59 schools suspended classes pre-emptively on Friday, most of them in the Mazovian province.
Tusk said police checks at schools would continue into next week. He also urged parents and teachers to talk to children about their online experiences and the consequences of becoming involved in online communities that glorify violence.
Authorities have not disclosed further details about the reported threat against Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz.

articles.title: A New Zealand man spent 11 years building a 370-metre miniature railway around his Whanganui home, with 1 - The Times of India
articles.summary: A New Zealand man spent 11 years building a 370-metre miniature railway around his Whanganui home, with 1  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Some home improvements are measured in fresh paint, landscaped gardens or a new kitchen. Ian Jones took a rather different approach. Over 11 years, the New Zealand retiree transformed his Whanganui property into a miniature railway world, complete with tunnels, bridges, stations and enough track to turn an ordinary residential section into a tiny transport network. Now, after years of building and tinkering, the property on Cornfoot Street in Castlecliff has a new owner. Sold for NZ$240,000, the home will remain connected to its most unusual feature, with the family buying it planning to keep the railway, states an online report by TradeMe.
From online find to backyard railway
The project began almost casually. Jones, who owns several properties in Whanganui, came across a child-sized petrol locomotive being sold online and decided to buy it. That small purchase eventually became the Nikau Junction Railway, a 370-metre miniature track winding through the property. What started as a whim grew steadily, with Jones adding 10 tunnels, two bridges, an artificial hill and two stations, adds the online report.
The complete circuit takes around 12 minutes to travel, with the track arranged in two interconnected loops. For visitors, the railway was more than an ornamental feature. 
It was a functioning ride built over years of hands-on work, the online report claims. The unusual property attracted national attention when it was listed earlier this year, with photographs putting the miniature railway front and centre.
A buyer willing to keep the trains
Finding someone who wanted both the property and its railway was never guaranteed. The listing generated considerable interest, but many prospective buyers were primarily interested in the land and viewed the elaborate railway as less important.
Eventually, the right match emerged. The new owners, a couple with a teenager, already have an unconventional living arrangement and plan to continue using the property in much the same spirit. They currently live in a bus and intend to sell it before moving the bus onto the Castlecliff property. The family also plans to retain the miniature railway, ensuring that Jones's 11-year project will continue under new ownership, adds the online report.
The sale price of NZ$240,000 was NZ$20,000 above the property's rateable value, a notable result in a market where some vacant sections have struggled to find buyers, the report mentions.
One railway, several chapters
For Jones, selling the property does not mean abandoning miniature railways. At 70, the retiree is already turning his attention to other interests, including renovating his own home, which had been neglected while much of his time went into the railway project.
He will also remain involved in trains through a friend's much larger model railway project near Castlecliff. The property is being developed into a wedding venue, giving Jones another opportunity to indulge his hobby without having to own the railway himself. During the sales process, prospective buyers could view the property by appointment. Some were even taken for rides, turning a conventional property inspection into something closer to a small attraction.
A quirky property finds its people
The Castlecliff home may have started as an ordinary residential property, but 11 years of work gave it a personality few listings can match. Its tunnels, bridges, stations and winding track transformed a piece of land into a miniature world. Now the railway has found owners who intend to keep it running. For Jones, the project moves into its next chapter, while the new family gets something considerably more unusual than a house: a home with its own railway network in the backyard.

articles.title: Climate Data Week: A confluence of domains, tech, and expectations - Fortune India
articles.summary: Climate Data Week: A confluence of domains, tech, and expectations  Fortune India
articles.full_text:
Does India need another climate week? Maybe yes and maybe no.
Climate change is a physical problem, but many of its solutions depend on solving a data problem. Glacier melt, flood prediction, energy demand, and renewable adoption all require us to collect and interpret vast amounts of data. The people who understand these challenges rarely collaborate with those building the data and AI systems.
Climate Data Week (CDW) is designed to close that gap: broader conversations that lead to data-backed solutions, and institutions that organise, share, and govern climate data well. It sets out to be an ecosystem catalyst through the collaborations it enables, the capital it attracts, and the policy attention it draws to climate challenges that go beyond borders. In the room: founders, researchers, corporate leaders, investors and policymakers. They leave with working partnerships, early sight of emerging categories, and evidence they can act on.
How can AI play a positive role in climate action?
There is enough general discourse about AI and climate; it is time to test real use cases. Illustratively, at the task level, AI helps in five ways: detecting faults in an electricity network; predicting demand; optimising the mix of wind, solar and storage; simulating scenarios; and discovering new materials for batteries and solar cells.
If we zoom out, the relationship between AI and climate spans four distinct pillars, each asking a different question:
1. AI for Climate Solutions: What can AI do for climate tech? Applications in products, operations, and assets that speed up decarbonisation, circularity, and resilience.
2. AI for Climate Intelligence: How can AI improve how we understand and govern climate? AI as a knowledge and decision layer: measurement, forecasting, MRV, risk assessment, and planning that inform governments, financiers and communities.
3. Sustainable AI: How can AI run on cleaner resources? Clean power for data centres, efficient water use, and lower lifecycle emissions across hardware supply chains.
4. Efficient AI: How can AI do more with less? Better algorithms, software and chips, judged against absolute demand, since a more efficient model that gets used ten times more is not necessarily a climate win.
Beyond a single domain
CDW’s conversations run across three themes: decarbonisation, adaptation and resilience, and circularity. Most forums treat them separately; they are intrinsically connected. Precise data helps cities find flood-prone areas and plan infrastructure. Accurate forecasting makes it easier to bring renewables onto the grid. And for farmers, timely data supports smarter decisions on irrigation and fertilisation as weather patterns shift. This first edition is built around those intersections: the four pillars give the programme its structure, and the three themes run across them.
Destination Bengaluru
Bengaluru attracts 58% of India’s AI startup funding, which makes it a natural home for the climate and data conversation. The real question is how that capability gets applied to problems that affect the planet and people’s lives. BLR-CDW 2026 is where we answer it.
Consider a founder building flood-prediction models for Indian cities and a researcher holding years of hydrological data that has never left the lab. The founder lacks reliable data; the researcher lacks a route to deployment. In the same room, they can agree on a pilot over a single cup of coffee (the rest, admittedly, takes longer). A corporation with flood exposure may become its first customer, an investor may spot the category early, and a policymaker may see the evidence working on a real map.
To make those connections happen, CDW brings together partners from across the climate, technology, and innovation ecosystem, including the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), Google, Climate Change AI, the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI), the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), and the U.S.-India Business Council.
CDW is also a place to learn from peers how climate data solutions go from pilot to scale, and it gives innovations grounded in local realities a global stage.
Why this matters for the Global South
Much of the current discourse on AI and climate centres on technologies built elsewhere. The Global South has its own climate problems, datasets, infrastructure constraints, and deployment realities, and it needs room to build and test solutions around local conditions; the approaches that emerge can serve other regions too.
Take, for instance, SatSure, a global Earth Intelligence company founded in Bengaluru in 2017, which turns satellite and aerial data into decision intelligence for agriculture, banking, and infrastructure. The company now has a presence across SE Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. Last year the company signed an MoU with the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO)—to use SatSure’s expertise for crop monitoring, yield forecasting, and climate resilience in Kenya.
Global technology players are also paying attention to innovative solutions in India. Google recently named four Indian startups—Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests, and Climitra Carbon—as part of the cohort for Google DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet in Asia-Pacific, a group of 16 organisations. Satellite-based land intelligence for small farmers, verified carbon removal, and agroforestry drone monitoring using AI are some of the areas in which these startups operate.
Measuring success by what it enables
So, back to the opening question: do we need another Climate Week? We think so, if its success is judged by what it enables: new collaborations, pathways from research to implementation, and opportunities for climate tech startups to scale.
Climate problems need people who can turn information into decisive action. AI and climate efforts must move beyond pilots to real collaboration on testing and deployment; that is how India puts its climate tech talent to work creating climate solutions worldwide.
(The author is co-founder, CCF. Views are personal.)
