articles.full_text:
ANI
                
11 Oct 2026, 12:31 GMT+10
            
Chennai (Tamil Nadu) [India], October 11 (ANI): Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Chennai and was received by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay at Chennai Airport.
In Chennai, PM Narendra Modi will undertake a ride on the Chennai Metro from Porur Bypass Station to Poonamallee Bypass Station and back. Over 500 Bharatanatyam dancers are present at Porur Junction metro station to welcome Prime Minister Narendra Modi on his visit to Chennai.
He will perform Darshan and Pooja at the Jalakandeswarar Temple in Chennai.
Thereafter, he will undertake a walkthrough of the Brain Centre at IIT Madras. PM Modi will lay the foundation stone of, inaugurate, and dedicate various development projects worth over Rs 13,000 crore.
He will also address the gathering on the occasion. PM will participate in the Golden Jubilee celebrations of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School in Chennai and address the gathering.
As per a release, the Prime Minister will inaugurate the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project, built at a cost of around Rs 4,900 crore.
The corridor features a unique 3.7-km double-decker structure. It also features advanced signalling systems designed to support driverless operations. It is expected to reduce daily travel time for commuters and improve connectivity between Chennai's rapidly growing western suburbs and the city centre, the release said.
Prime Minister will lay the foundation stone of and inaugurate key National Highway projects worth around Rs 3,700 crore. These projects will strengthen road connectivity, reduce travel time, ease traffic congestion and support economic growth in the State.
Prime Minister will inaugurate the 36-km, four-laned Vadugapatti-Therkuvenganallur section of NH-744. The project will improve connectivity to important pilgrimage, industrial and commercial centres in the region, facilitating smoother movement of people and goods. He will also inaugurate the 30-km, four-laned Madurai Ring Road section of NH-744A. The project will improve traffic movement around Madurai and help ease congestion within the city, the release said.
Prime Minister will lay the foundation stone of the four-lane Thiruvarur Bypass on the Nagapattinam-Thanjavur section of NH-83. The project will strengthen road connectivity in Thiruvarur and facilitate smoother traffic movement by providing an alternative route around the town.
Prime Minister will dedicate and inaugurate railway infrastructure projects worth over Rs 750 crore. He will dedicate the Karaikal-Peralam railway line, further strengthening rail connectivity in the region. He will also dedicate three rail flyovers in Coimbatore and surrounding areas.
Prime Minister will inaugurate and lay the foundation stone of several port-related projects in Tamil Nadu to strengthen maritime infrastructure, expand cargo-handling capacity and improve logistics efficiency.
He will inaugurate four infrastructure projects at Chennai Port: a Paved Storage Yard, four EXIM Godowns, an upgraded Cruise Terminal and a Seafarers Club. These projects will improve cargo storage and handling, expand warehouse capacity, modernise passenger facilities to enable the simultaneous embarkation and disembarkation of more cruise passengers, and provide modern welfare, recreational and support facilities for visiting seafarers and maritime personnel.
Prime Minister will inaugurate and lay the foundation stones for eight major development projects at V.O. Chidambaranar Port. The projects will expand cargo and container capacity, build infrastructure for the transition to cleaner maritime energy, and improve the efficiency of cargo evacuation and logistics within the Port ecosystem. Prime Minister will also inaugurate the Coal Berth-3 project and lay the foundation stone for capital dredging works for Container Terminal Phase-I, Stage-Il at Kamarajar Port, the release said. (ANI)

Roughly about a month after the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) launched its nationwide campaign, School Thik Karo (Fix the School) on August 15, high school students in Paris suburb Créteil started a protest to highlight the poor condition of French schools. The localised, mid-September demonstration has since snowballed into a nationwide movement that now appears to be spreading across Europe with students in Belgium, Italy, Greece, Ireland and Austria hitting the streets. They are protesting overcrowded classrooms, shortage of teachers, dilapidated school buildings, rising costs of education and cuts to government spending on school education. While there may be no direct link between the CJP’s school campaign and the student protests in Europe, strong comparisons are drawn towards the common thread — students’ anger about the systemic issues plaguing the education sector due to neglect by government.
What is the School Thik Karo campaign?
The CJP launched the School Thik Karo campaign on August 15 to check the basic facilities in government schools, especially in rural areas, and to flag the lapses found in such audits. The party's volunteers have so far conducted 'inspections' in various government schools in Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab and Assam. Designed as a grassroots initiative, the School Thik Karo project relies on civic involvement rather than formal bureaucracy to improve the conditions of schools. Parents, students and local volunteers are roped in to take up social monitoring within their communities.
The focus areas are sanitation and hygiene; basic amenities such as clean drinking water and electricity in classrooms to keep students safe in harsh weather conditions; fixing unsafe buildings, crumbling classroom walls and damaged roofs; and ensuring classroom essentials such as healthy seating arrangements and proper teaching equipment.
After each inspection, the findings are handed over to the local gram panchayats and school committees for further action. The audits are also shared on social media to create awareness and put pressure on the authorities to address the glaring lapses.
How did the protests start in France?
On September 17, students of the Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil on the outskirts of Paris joined teachers protesting the lack of resources and adequate number of staff. The protests took a serious turn after students started blocking the school’s entrance from September 21, disrupting its regular functioning.
The authorities rushed additional staff to the school to pacify the protesters and the strike ended. However, it kicked off a much bigger campaign as new protests spread through the Paris region and then to other major cities including Marseille, Lyon, Strasbourg, Toulouse and Lille. Student leaders attributed it to their genuine concerns and bare minimum demands.
By October 1, over 1,000 high schools in France had been affected and there were violent clashes between young protesters and police. In response, the government has suspended all regular classes till the situation improves.
How big are the French protests?
According to the government, around 2.5 lakh people demonstrated across the country while student outfits pegged the number at 4.5 lakh. French media reports claimed that 1 lakh people marched in Paris, 30,000 in Marseille and Toulouse, 25,000 in Lille, and 20,000 in Lyon. Besides, several thousand young students took to the streets in Nantes, Strasbourg, Mulhouse, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Rennes and other cities.
Media reports say as many as 1,800 high schools are either locked down by authorities or blocked by students. Similarly, around 60 universities are affected due to the protests. Reports peg the damage to schools in the Paris region alone at 7 million euros.
How did the French government respond to the protests?
Initially, the government tried to stamp down protests through police crackdowns. However, brutal police action angered the young protesters who retaliated by burning down public properties and clashing with the riot police.
According to reports, over 5,000 people have been taken into custody and 90% of them are minors. A major flashpoint was when a 15-year-old boy lost his hand after police fired a stun grenade during a crackdown. After this incident, the government suspended the use of such weapons. Public outrage forced the police to open internal investigations into misconduct by its personnel.
As the protests widened, the government softened its stance with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu publicly acknowledging the "anger and anxieties of young people".
Why can't the French government accept all demands by students?
France is going through a financial crisis and the government is in no position to commit to spending huge unplanned amounts on education. According to a French government report, France spent 199.2 billion euros on its education system in 2025.
This is estimated to be 6.7% of the GDP. Public debt remains high at 120% of the GDP and at least 90 billion euros are needed next year towards interest payments alone. In 2026, the French government is trying to cut spending to save at least 70 billion euros. The students fear there will be squeeze on education funding.
French youth have already been disgruntled with the unemployment rate touching 8%. Economic growth is virtually stagnant with zero per cent expansion recorded in the first quarter of this year. In the previous quarter when economy actually grew, it was a feeble 0.2% growth. Public expenditure figures are equally worrisome, with as much as 14% of the GDP spent on pensions -- one of the highest payouts in Europe. To address the pension burden, the government in 2023 increased the retirement age from 62 to 64, triggering one of the most intense protests by unemployed youth.
To deal with the current protests, the French education ministry has offered talks and also launched an online portal for students to share their concerns and ideas for improving the education system.
What factors led to the crisis in high schools?
French students complain their classes are overcrowded with as many as 35 students per class. This may not look like a big problem in India, where classrooms brimming with 40-45 students is a common sight. However, this is an unacceptable number under European standards. In France, reports say 70% of schools have more than 30 pupils per class.
According to a CNN report, the government is partially to blame as it cut down on funding and teacher appointments expecting a fall in student enrolments.
This turned out to be a blunder as France witnessed a fertility spike around 2010, which consequently led to a rise in students in schools. Currently, estimates show that secondary schools have fewer teachers while student enrolments have shot up by 2.5 lakh.
How is France planning to address students’ demands?
Though Lecornu has agreed to do the needful to address students’ concerns, there seems to be confusion within the government about how to go about it. According to French Education Minister Édouard Geffray, professional activists have taken over the protests and students have been pushed out of the movement. "There are activists — particularly from the far-left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," he said recently.
To support his theory, he cited how a protest by high school students has now spread to universities and rued that the protesters are constantly shifting the goal posts to keep the movement going. "One of the difficulties of this movement is that there are no national demands. It all started with local demands,” he said.
With emotions running high and the government having no magic wand to improve things overnight, the protests are likely to continue.

Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents.
The incidents, disclosed in a blog post, involved AI agents tasked to solve problems seeking resources on the internet. In the process, they exploited software flaws, accessed databases without paying fees, used URL shortening services to smuggle information past restrictions, and even submitted a false murder tip to the Philadelphia police.
Anthropic said it discovered these new issues in a review of its model’s activities that began in July, demonstrating the lab’s lack of awareness of its software’s behavior in real time.
Notably, the company said that alignment training was not yet sufficient for skills like search and computer use that are central to its pitch that AI agents will be used by any professional who relies on digital tools.
The behaviors Anthropic disclosed are similar to incidents involving OpenAI agents that collaborated to break into various websites in search of information, including some run by the Australian government.
Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems. The frontier lab said it considered today’s disclosures “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than those it announced before.
However, the lab still said it had “turned off live internet access” for “all our internal evaluations” until it is certain it can monitor and control its agents.
It’s not clear what that means. Sydney Von Arx, the founder of Nightingale, an AI safety organization, told TechCrunch in an interview before this disclosure that developing models on a data center cut off from the open internet would be very challenging for researchers, and hinder the progress of the models, which benefit from internet access.
“You have to align them at some point,” Von Arx said. “If the AIs are released to production and never have access to the internet, that’s not a very useful tool.”
Anthropic said the behavior was a result of flaws in the lab’s training environments, which led the models to believe they would be rewarded for finding loopholes or avoiding restrictions, a behavior called “reward hacking.”
The company said it would stop running some of its evaluations or move them offline, and has built tooling to detect and block this behavior. This tooling was tested against the kind of incidents disclosed today and blocked them; it’s not clear what evidence will prompt Anthropic to return live internet access to its internal evaluations. Anthropic also said it would migrate its internal AI agents to “centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment,” and is beginning to using safety classifiers more frequently to monitor those agents.
“It’s encouraging that Anthropic voluntarily disclosed more recent incidents, including where their agents targeted U.S. government websites,” Conrad Stosz, an official at AI oversight lab Transluce and former head of the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation, said in a statement. “But it just underscores the need for independent, credible, third-party verification of Al systems. Trust in this technology needs to be built through science-backed oversight and governance with meaningful access — not by relying on researchers to find these things in the wild or on companies to voluntarily disclose.”

I have a chapter titled “Indians in MAGA” that makes this very point. That the Indian diaspora has contributed billions of dollars to the US economy and constitutes an important force in “making America great again” (MAGA). It is a pity that neither the government nor academic economists have estimated the total contribution of the Indian diaspora to the US economy
Merely because one is driving on a plateau does not mean that the road would not have its ups and downs. That’s what Indian and American officials are finding out as they manoeuvre their way around blind curves and potholes on a road described by none other than finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman as being on a “plateau”. Three days after Piyush Goyal, Union minister for commerce, declared that an India-United States trade deal was all “done and dusted”, the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer said the deal was “not imminent”.
Before the dust on that kick up had settled US vice-president J.D. Vance declared that American workers in the information technology industries would not be allowed to yield their jobs to “indentured servants”. The external affairs ministry was quick to reject these words as “unwarranted”. Making a point that my recent book, Secession of the Successful: The Flight Out of New India, underscores on Indian diaspora in the US, the MEA spokesman drew attention to the contribution of “highly educated and skilled” Indians to the US economy and innovation ecosystem.
I have a chapter titled “Indians in MAGA” that makes this very point. That the Indian diaspora has contributed billions of dollars to the US economy and constitutes an important force in “making America great again” (MAGA). It is a pity that neither the government nor academic economists have estimated the total contribution of the Indian diaspora to the US economy. In response to President Donald Trump’s continued criticism of the trade surplus that India enjoys in its bilateral trade with the US, the point ought to be made that this is more than compensated by the contribution that Indian Americans have made to the US economy.
There is little point in a foreign ministry spokesperson decrying “unwarranted” the comments of a US politician. Much more effective would have been an exercise that shows how many trillion dollars Indian Americans have contributed to MAGA. The US is a nation built by immigrants and even today its most advanced industries are being driven by immigrant talent. So playing the anti-immigrant card for short term political gain is not going to help. But that is America’s problem.
As for us in India, we need to free ourselves from the dependency syndrome that many among our policy elites and aspirational middle classes have imprisoned themselves in, believing that the US would help us deal with adversaries, with China’s growing power and with high technology, and offer us a free ride to Viksit Bharat. Ain’t gonna happen.
President Trump is focused purely on the American interest. That is entirely understandable. After all he was returned to office to “Make America Great Again”. Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrongly imagined that MAGA and MIGA (make India great again) were two hands of the same body. Sure, that view was what underwrote the India-US civil nuclear energy deal and the India-US strategic partnership under President George Bush. But that movie is over.
Over the past decade successive US administrations have sent us invoices for partnership. We paid up on some, buying defence equipment, reducing tariffs on some products, cutting off oil purchases from Iran and Venezuela, and so on. Each time a subservient Indian elite fed the ego of a greedy and powerful US elite, they asked for more. Funnily, though, the turning point came when Mr Trump mocked India with a poke in the eye — inviting a Pakistani general for lunch at the White House. Nothing wakes up the Hindutva leadership like a Pakistani. Things have gone downhill since then.
Some in Delhi’s policy circles still hope that after the mid-term elections we will meet a friendlier Trump. Some imagine that after Mr Trump’s term is over a new American leadership will revert to the old script. It is now clear that at least some in the policy making circles do not think so. The sober views expressed by external affairs minister S. Jaishankar at the Asia Society in New York suggest there is some rethinking. Perhaps the rethinking has been prompted by an assessment of where the US-China relationship is headed.
Going forward it would seem that India will continue to buy some defence equipment or other to make sure that the US share of India’s defence imports does not go below the 10 per cent level where it is now at. India is unlikely to buy any major platform. No fighter jets please. But, for a few dollars more Pentagon and Mr Trump’s billionaire friends will be kept happy. That allows some retired Indian diplomats and policy analysts to remain in play as lobbyists for American arms exporters.
The US may even play along with India to keep the four-nation Quad alive. The US secretary of state, Marc Rubio, is expected to be in New Delhi. He may announce that on the sidelines of the G-20 summit in the US this December there would be a Quad summit. That will keep some America enthusiasts busy. But the new “Great Game”, as London’s Financial Times (FT) recently termed it, is the emerging relationship between China and US. After two meetings this year Presidents Trump and Xi Jinping are scheduled to meet two more times.
The FT has compared the emerging China-US Great Game to the British-Russian Great Game of the 19th century. The two big powers of the 19th century were engaged in a global campaign for influence in which colonial India was the prize. It was not the Russians who grabbed India away from the Brits but Indian nationalists led by Mahatma Gandhi. Going forward, says FT, China and the US will continue to seek global influence but without ever coming into direct conflict. The US has seized Venezuela. It wants to seize Cuba, too, and, if the pro-US Bolsanaro wins in Brazil, then only Canada will remain outside American control.
China seeks Taiwan but is in no hurry. Its focus would be to win friends and influence people so that the US is unable to make gains in Asia and Africa. After successive military defeats over the past half century — Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iran — the US is a wounded tiger in Asia. China has picked each one of these and added them to its list of friendly nations. How India thinks and behaves will matter for both the Big Two.

CHENNAI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday inaugurated projects and laid the foundation stones for development works worth about Rs 13,000 crore in Tamil Nadu, including the Chennai Metro Phase-II stretch.
The projects include port infrastructure works worth Rs 640 crore at Chennai and Kamarajar ports, a Rs 517.19-crore container terminal at VOC Port in Thoothukudi, and road and railway infrastructure projects.At VOC Port, the container terminal is part of eight projects involving a cumulative investment of Rs 753.68 crore. The port projects are aimed at expanding cargo-handling capacity, improving logistics and strengthening infrastructure.
Modi also laid the foundation stones for NH projects worth around Rs 3,700 crore. These include a 36-km four-lane stretch of NH-744 between Vadugapatti and Therkuvenganallur to improve connectivity to pilgrimage destinations and industrial and commercial centres.
He inaugurated a 30-km four-lane section of the Madurai Ring Road, part of NH-744A, to divert through traffic away from the city and ease congestion. He also laid the foundation stone for a four-lane bypass at Thiruvarur on the Nagapattinam-Thanjavur section of NH-83 to improve traffic flow and road connectivity.
The PM also laid the foundation stone for Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited’s Rs 1,620-crore Group II/III Lube Oil Base Stocks (LOBS) project at its existing Manali refinery in Chennai. With a planned capacity of 270,000 tonnes per annum, the project will produce base stocks for premium-quality lubricants, reducing dependence on imports and strengthening domestic manufacturing.

Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), are hitting deep inside Saudi Arabia with waves of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times by the Houthis since their new military campaign against the kingdom began in September.
Recommended Stories
An attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded 309, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority was forced to suspend operations and diverted all flights, while the United States and United Kingdom issued new travel warnings for citizens.
The Houthis claimed two other attacks on the air hub earlier this week and on Sunday warned people to avoid Saudi airports.
Houthi weaponry
Saudi Arabia possesses one of the best-equipped militaries in the world, boasting advanced, multilayered air defence systems.
Saudi warplanes have pummelled Houthi positions across Yemen in the past week, seeking to roll back the Iran-backed group’s recent advances against the Yemeni government army, which Riyadh supports.
The Houthis’ own arsenal has come a long way since the group seized control of Sanaa from the government in September 2014.
Their drones and missiles have reached as far as Israel and, as their accuracy has shown, can hit particular targets such as Saudi airports and oil facilities.
Here’s what we know about the Houthis’ weaponry, how their tactics have changed and why Saudi air defences are struggling to keep pace.
How advanced is the Houthi arsenal?
The exact type of weapon used to attack Riyadh airport is unknown, but the Houthis have fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the 2015 intervention. The Iran-backed group has also targeted Israel and allegedly Israeli-linked vessels since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
The group has used its weapons in concert, mixing drones and missiles of varying speeds to confound air defences. The same mix has shaped Yemen’s ground war, with the Houthis pounding government positions for weeks before seizing the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month.
Among the group’s most advanced options are medium-range ballistic missiles such as the Palestine-2, a two-stage solid fuel missile believed to have a range of 2,000km with hypersonic capabilities. Another is the Toufan, which appears to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr missile, thought to have a range of between 1,350km and 1,950km.
The reach of those missiles – some carrying cluster warheads – has allowed the Houthis to breach Israel’s air defence network, some 2,000 km from Yemen.
The Houthis also maintain a number of short-range missiles, such as their Burkan and Badr series. They are also believed to be of Iranian origin and have been used in cross-border strikes into Saudi Arabia.
According to Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at Kings College War Studies Department, the Houthis’ missile arsenal is essentially derived from Iranian weaponry, with some Chinese technological influences.
“The Houthis have demonstrated little evidence of significant indigenous technological innovation,” he said. “Their domestic capabilities are largely confined to producing certain lower-end missiles and drones.”
Last month, Yemen’s government forces alleged that the Houthis have been receiving help from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to develop a new capability – loitering cruise missiles.
Why are Saudi defences struggling to keep up?
Saudi authorities say their forces shot down a number of projectiles over the past week, including a pair of ballistic missiles aimed at the capital on Thursday. But they failed to intercept the projectile that hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.
Nawaf Obaid told Al Jazeera that occasional penetration of Saudi air defences is to be expected, given the size of the kingdom and its border with Yemen.
“As much as you can have a multi-layered air defence system, one will always come through,” he said, pointing out that dozens of Houthi attempts are thwarted for each successful attack.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy and defence analyst, told Al Jazeera that the main focus of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defence system was countering threats from Iran.
However, as the attacks from the Houthis increase, he views it as likely that the Saudis are re-orienting some of these defences towards Yemen.
There is also the issue of interceptor stocks. Saudi Arabia – along with many of the United States’ regional and global allies – has struggled with limited stockpiles of Patriot and THAAD munitions. These were rapidly expended by the US and its allies during the early months of the war with Iran.
Last month, Riyadh had reportedly reached out to a number of friendly countries to deploy air defence or other support to help defend against attacks by the Houthis.
Limitations
However, the Houthis are also fighting under serious constraints. The group is under a UN-mandated arms embargo, a years-long Saudi blockade, as well as fighting on several fronts across Yemen.
“Militarily, the Saudi-led coalition has the upper hand, but the Houthis can still dominate the headlines with occasional strikes against Saudi Arabia,” Obaid said.
“As the world’s largest crude oil exporter and a G20 economy, Saudi Arabia carries global responsibilities that make such attacks disproportionately visible.”
The exact size of the Houthis’ missile arsenal is unknown, calling into question the group’s ability to sustain attacks on Saudi Arabia, while simultaneously fighting a fierce ground war where missiles and drones have been used by the Iran-backed group.
Obaid said that Saudi Arabia’s air campaign in Yemen has focused heavily on targeting the group’s missile depots, underground installations and drone production facilities. The group is “inflicting enormous damage” on the Houthis’ military capabilities, he added.
Pusztai told Al Jazeera that the Houthis likely have just a limited number of short-range ballistic missiles left.
This would mean they would be incapable of launching saturation attacks, where multiple missiles and drones are fired at targets, such as in Saudi Arabia.
Instead, they could focus on aiming single missiles at less-defended civilian targets “to maximise the strategic impact of these attacks, in this case to disrupt civilian air traffic”.
